history.headline: County crews abandon reservoir inspection after equipment failure
history.text: A county inspection crew found an upright white structure standing behind the reservoir pump building. It measured approximately nineteen feet from the ground to its highest visible point. Six folded projections extended from its back. A tractor stalled forty feet away. The crew left the site when every work light failed in sequence. No injuries were reported.

history.headline: Two confirmed dead following West End Laundromat emergency
history.text: Emergency workers recovered two bodies at West End Laundromat. Both were found standing against a locked service door. The medical examiner reported that their clothing was fused to the painted metal. The victims had been heard knocking from inside the wall after the building was evacuated. The structure is closed, and June Mercer was hospitalized following exposure.

history.headline: Resident killed after library corridor sealed itself
history.text: Ernest Pike was confirmed dead in an incident at Bramhollow Library. A corridor wall was found extending through a doorway that had been open minutes earlier. His body was located on the opposite side without any break in the plaster. A maintenance worker said the wall was still warm. The library has closed until further notice.

turns.text: Harold, The Reservoir Stilt. Why a stilt?
Tall. Reservoir. It’s got a spine to it, unlike a coat that’s apparently wandered off a bus.
You’re proud of that? You’ve named a thing you never saw after the nearest puddle.
Reservoir. Not puddle. Words do matter, Sam.
Harold has mistaken a longer word for a better thought.
And you’ve named it The Blank Sleeve. You’ve managed to make a sleeve sound unemployed.
It is a description, not a job reference.
Ellen, why that name?
It’s spare. The shape was tall, according to Sam; a sleeve suggests a person without pretending we know there was one.
I didn’t say sleeve. I said it was there.
Then we need a vote. A proper one. I’ll put a box by the register Saturday.
You’ll put a box by the register so every customer has to see you winning.
I’m open longer than you are. That’s called convenience.
It’s also called having your own ballot box beside the nails.
Sam, would a vote bother you?
The name doesn’t bother me. It’s that patch of road. I can still point to it without looking.
That doesn’t make it—
Don’t finish that for me.
Harold, you say your name sounds less foolish. Are you worried people are laughing at the name, or at you?
I’m worried you’re helping them do both. The Reservoir Stilt has a shape to it. The others sound like things Sam’s misplaced.
I haven’t misplaced anything. And I didn’t offer garden supplies so you could use me as your example of a town fool.
I didn’t say that. You’re the one making every sentence sound like a personal injury.
Harold, you could make a compliment sound like an invoice.
You’ve been waiting all week to say that.
No. I thought of it just now. It’s worse for you that way.
Sam, does the garden offer have anything to do with wanting the town to take you seriously?
It has to do with the garden needing supplies. That’s all. I don’t need a prize for lending things.
No, you just need everyone to call it The Long Coat.
I didn’t ask everyone to do anything. You’re the one trying to turn this into a contest.
A name is a contest the minute people start choosing sides.
Then stop standing there with a little flag in your hand.
I have no flag. I have a hardware store. People know what I sell.
I know what I saw. I don’t know what it was. Those aren’t the same thing.
When you pass Reservoir Road now, do you look for it?
No. I look away before I get there. Then I wonder why I did.
That still doesn’t make it a—
The county bulletin says nineteen feet. I want to make sure I read that correctly.
You did. Nineteen feet is not a bad measurement. That's the part I keep hearing.
You weren't at the reservoir this morning, Sam?
No. I know what I saw by Reservoir Road before. I didn't see this thing they found.
And neither did I. I'm not going to pretend I did just because a bulletin has numbers in it.
Good. The numbers are already alarming enough without adding your imagination.
There you go. Can't let a serious evening pass without correcting me.
The tractor stalled forty feet away. The bulletin doesn't say why.
And the lights went out one by one. That's a crew standing there watching the light go away.
It says they left. I keep thinking about how long it took to get out of there in the dark.
We don't know how long. The county hasn't said.
Then don't make it worse by filling in the parts nobody knows.
You used to fill in plenty when it was only my word against yours.
This isn't about that now.
No. It isn't. We have the bulletin in front of us, and that's all we can confirm tonight.
We have the county bulletin in front of us. Two people are dead. June Mercer is hospitalized following exposure.
I heard the words. I don't know what to do with them.
They were standing at the door. That's what the bulletin says. Standing there.
Against a locked service door. And their clothing was fused to the metal. Please don't make it sound less terrible by leaving out the words.
I wasn't trying to make it less terrible.
The bulletin says knocking was heard from inside the wall after the building was evacuated. We don't know more than that.
Somebody got out of that building and still had to hear knocking. I keep trying to picture leaving.
Don't picture a person the bulletin doesn't identify. We know two people died. We don't know their names.
Right. Sorry. Two people. And June's in the hospital.
I know that place. I've sold soap to people going there. You walk in to get clean. I don't have anything useful to say.
No. None of us has an explanation.
Then say that. Don't turn it into a riddle. Two people are dead.
Yesterday I was arguing about what to call something I saw by the road. That feels stupid now.
It wasn't stupid then. But I'm done arguing about the name tonight.
We have no confirmed reopening time for the laundromat. We will read the bulletin again if we need to. I'm sorry. I—let's keep the line open.
The county says Ernest Pike is dead. Ellen, I know the library is your workplace. Were you there tonight?
No. I wasn't there. I want that clear. I read the bulletin like everybody else.
It says the wall crossed the doorway. His body was on the other side.
Without a break in the plaster. Yes. Those words are already bad enough.
And the wall was warm. That's not a sentence I ever expected to hear about the library.
I don't know what you're supposed to do with that. I don't know what to say.
You could stop trying to make it sound ordinary.
I'm not. I'm trying not to say something stupid.
Three confirmed deaths now. One today. Ernest Pike is named in the bulletin.
Yesterday it was that laundromat. Today the library. You go to those places because they're just there.
People came in to return books. They came in to sit somewhere quiet. I keep thinking about the books still on the carts.
Ellen, I'm sorry. I don't know what to—
My store's open in the morning. That's all I can tell you. I don't know if anyone should go anywhere.
Don't tell people it's safe because you don't know what else to tell them.
I didn't say safe, Sam.
No. You didn't. We have the bulletin. The library is closed. I'm sorry, we'll—just give me a moment.
